title: The Head of Department Manifesto 2026
author: Salles, Dominic
source: Dominic Salles' School Improvement Newsletter (dominicsalles.substack.com), September 9,
summary: In this opening chapter of a planned 40-chapter manifesto for department heads, Dominic Salles argues that new subject leaders default to imitating whichever school leaders impressed or disappointed them personally, when they should instead be analyzing every past leader — likable or not — strictly through the lens of measurable impact on student learning. His organizing device is 'Bartlett's Five Buckets' (what you know, what you can do, your network, your resources, your reputation), ranked in a deliberate order because, he argues, only knowledge and skill survive a genuine professional crisis; the other three can be stripped away by circumstance. He illustrates the method with his own worked example: analyzing a likable but dishonest former headteacher not for his character flaws but for the specific mechanisms (staff socializing, strong arts programs) that produced low staff turnover and a stable school community. The chapter's underlying claim is that leadership development should start from cold analysis of 'what worked, and how was it led,' stripped of personality judgments, rather than from inherited folklore about inspirational versus uninspiring leaders.
points: Ranks 'what you know' and 'what you can do' above network, resources, and reputation because only the first two survive a genuine professional crisis.
Argues new leaders should analyze even leaders they personally disliked, asking only 'what worked, and how was it led,' stripped of personality judgment.
Uses the fact that teacher variation within a school exceeds variation between schools to argue leadership impact is about ordinary practice, not exceptional individuals.
Frames 'being good with people' as insufficient by itself — the only real answer to what makes a leader successful is measurable impact on learning.

Worked example: a dishonest but sociable former headteacher retained staff and built community not through integrity but through concrete practices (forced socializing, a strong arts program) worth extracting and reusing.
quotes: There will be leaders who have upset and disappointed you – you'll have an idea of what not to do. You will also have a range of role models visibly behaving as leaders.
It is a truism that the variation between teachers in your own school is far greater than the variation between schools. That is why about 70% of schools have average Progress 8.

There are only two buckets that any … professional earthquake can never empty – it can take away your network, it can take your resources, it can even impact your reputation, but it can never remove your knowledge and it can never remove your skills.
So being inspirational and brilliant with people is not the answer. The answer is always impact on learning. You need to reflect on your experience – what only you know – through the lens of impact.

My first head teacher was very sociable, but dishonest. He would lie about anything to get his own way, or just for fun, but he was still very likeable. The school did well because teachers stayed and became part of the community.
The takeaway is always, 'what did they do that led to the success'. Even leaders who you don't like will have succeeded in improving learning in some way.
